content: The comparative effectiveness of two injectable agents has been a focus of research, particularly due to evidence of permanent effects linked to their toxicity. This has driven the development of new treatment approaches, including shorter, injectable-sparing regimens. For example, the South African Department of Health shared observational data with the World Health Organization (WHO) on a 9-month, all-oral regimen containing bedaquiline. Since 2019, WHO has recommended this regimen, which includes a combination of medicines such as bedaquiline, levofloxacin (or moxifloxacin), ethionamide, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, high-dose isoniazid, and clofazimine. In 2022, new evidence from South Africa led to a modification of this regimen, replacing 4 months of ethionamide with 2 months of linezolid (600 mg daily). The need for more effective treatments for patients with extensive drug resistance, including fluoroquinolone resistance, has prompted numerous studies to evaluate novel regimens. One of the first such studies was the Nix-TB trial, conducted by the TB Alliance. This Phase III, open-label, observational cohort study assessed the safety, efficacy, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of a 6-month BPaL regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid), extendable to 9 months for specific cases. Conducted in South Africa between 2014 and 2019, the study provided evidence reviewed by WHO in 2019, leading to recommendations for the use of the BPaL regimen under operational research conditions for pre-XDR-TB patients. Two randomized controlled trials, TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix, concluded in 2021, offering new evidence that prompted WHO to reassess and update its recommendations for MDR/RR-TB treatment. The ZeNix trial specifically evaluated the BPaL regimen with linezolid (600 mg daily for 26 weeks) in patients with MDR/RR-TB, with or without fluoroquinolone resistance. This was compared to a cohort treated with a 9-month regimen including linezolid for 2 months. The evidence from these studies remains uncertain due to limitations such as small sample sizes, confounding biases, and differences in trial versus programmatic settings. The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly disrupted TB services, reversing years of progress. There was an 18% global decline in newly diagnosed and reported TB cases in 2020, returning to 2012 levels. This reduced access to diagnosis and treatment has led to increased TB-related deaths. For drug-resistant TB, the number of people receiving treatment dropped by 15% between 2019 and 2020, with only about one-third of those in need receiving care. However, treatment success rates for MDR/RR-TB have improved globally, reaching 59% in 2018 compared to 50% in 2012. Shorter and more effective treatment regimens for drug-resistant TB are urgently needed to improve outcomes, reduce adverse events, and prevent further drug resistance. The BPaL regimen, with its shorter duration and reduced pill burden, aligns with these goals. However, challenges remain, including the need for drug susceptibility testing and safety monitoring, as well as limited availability of certain drugs. The WHO panel judged the BPaL regimen to have large desirable effects and moderate undesirable effects compared to the 9-month regimen. Despite very low certainty of evidence, the panel determined that the balance of health effects probably favors the BPaL regimen. The intervention is considered acceptable to key stakeholders, including patients and healthcare providers, and feasible to implement, given its reduced complexity and duration. However, resource requirements and cost-effectiveness remain areas of uncertainty. In conclusion, WHO recommends the use of the 6-month BPaL regimen (bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid) over the 9-month regimen for patients with MDR/RR-TB without fluoroquinolone resistance, provided they have not been previously exposed to bedaquiline and linezolid for more than one month. This recommendation is based on the potential benefits of shorter treatment duration, improved outcomes, and reduced burden on patients and healthcare systems.
